lessons.title: SSRI-associated hyponatremia / possible SIADH
lessons.opening: An older patient taking sertraline and a diuretic develops new weakness and unsteadiness. What medication-related risk belongs in your differential?
facts: SSRIs can cause hyponatremia, often associated with SIADH. Older age, diuretic use and volume depletion raise risk. Symptomatic hyponatremia requires stopping sertraline and appropriate medical intervention.
gaps: Do not diagnose SIADH from medication exposure alone. Full diagnostic criteria and correction protocols are not loaded.

lessons.opening: A metformin-treated patient with eGFR 50 is scheduled for iodinated contrast. What does this product label require?

lessons.title: Confusion, falls and polypharmacy
lessons.opening: A 76-year-old woman with depression, hypertension and osteoarthritis has new unsteadiness and difficulty concentrating. Sertraline was recently increased; she also takes a diuretic and uses OTC pain remedies. She lives alone. Give a one-sentence problem representation and identify the first safety concern.
reveals: After the initial differential: simulated sodium is 124 mmol/L; glucose 106 mg/dL.
After discussing next tests: baseline sodium was 138 one month earlier; oral intake has been poor. Serum/urine osmolality and volume assessment are not yet available.
Before the plan: she prioritizes staying independent and has difficulty arranging transportation.
facts: Sertraline-associated hyponatremia is a source-supported possible contributor; the case does not establish SIADH or exclude other causes.
gaps: Full hyponatremia differential, diagnostic thresholds and treatment protocols need additional evidence. No correction-rate teaching from this case.

lessons.title: Kidney function decline with competing chronic treatments
lessons.opening: A 68-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and CKD reports poor intake and new dizziness. His list includes metformin, lisinopril, a diuretic and recently added OTC ibuprofen. What links these details, and what needs attention first?
reveals: After the differential: simulated creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL compared with 1.2 previously; current reported eGFR is 28.
After test planning: he is still taking all listed medicines and cannot name the OTC doses.
Before the plan: he fears losing blood pressure control if medicines are changed and has limited access to repeat laboratory testing.
facts: Medication exposure and volume depletion may contribute; do not assume a single cause. Metformin renal restrictions and the ACE inhibitor/NSAID warning are loaded.
gaps: A full AKI diagnostic/management guideline is not loaded. eGFR during changing renal function requires caution; do not turn the value into an automated dose calculator.

lessons.title: Fatigue and possible bleeding during anticoagulation
lessons.opening: An 82-year-old woman with nonvalvular AF, CKD and arthritis reports new fatigue and easy bruising. She takes apixaban and recently added OTC ibuprofen. How do you prioritize the differential and immediate assessment?
reveals: After initial assessment: simulated weight is 58 kg and serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL; she reports taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily.
After discussing tests: simulated hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL compared with 12.0 previously; she then reports dark stools.
Before the plan: she strongly fears another stroke and is worried about medication costs.
facts: Reconcile the anticoagulant indication and AF reduction criteria. Medication risks do not by themselves prove the bleeding source.
gaps: GI bleeding diagnosis, transfusion thresholds, interruption/reversal and restarting anticoagulation require additional guideline evidence. Prioritize escalation reasoning without inventing a protocol.

lessons.title: Heart failure, CKD and a complicated medication transition
lessons.opening: A 70-year-old man with reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure, hypertension and CKD brings conflicting medication lists after a care transition. Lisinopril, spironolactone, potassium supplements and a new sacubitril/valsartan order all appear. What must you clarify before recommending a plan?
reveals: After reconciliation: he took lisinopril this morning and has not started the new prescription.
After targeted testing: simulated potassium is 5.4 mEq/L and eGFR is 38.
Before the plan: he cannot afford frequent laboratory visits and wants the simplest workable schedule.
facts: The ACE inhibitor/ARNI transition and potassium-raising therapy require separate safety assessments. Avoid treating every combination as an absolute contraindication.
gaps: Comprehensive heart failure sequencing, emergency potassium management and sacubitril/valsartan dosing need additional evidence.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Renal table: adults and pediatric patients aged at least 3 months weighing greater than 40 kg; not a renal protocol for smaller children.
contraindications: Serious prior hypersensitivity to amoxicillin or another beta-lactam is a labeled contraindication.

renal.guidance: Label uses GFR in mL/min: below 30, avoid the 875 mg dose. At GFR 10-30 use 250 or 500 mg every 12 hours; below 10, every 24 hours, depending on infection severity. This is an organ-adjustment reference, not a replacement indication-specific regimen.

hepatic.guidance: No quantitative hepatic adjustment is established in the loaded sections.

monitoring: Assess allergy history and renal function before applying the supported regimen.
gaps: Do not infer hepatic safety from a missing adjustment. Dialysis and smaller-child renal dosing need a separately scoped regimen; interactions are not comprehensively loaded.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Oral penicillin V; retain CDC strep indication and population.
contraindications: Previous hypersensitivity to a penicillin is a labeled contraindication.

renal.guidance: The label describes delayed elimination in kidney impairment but supplies no quantitative renal adjustment in this extract.

hepatic.guidance: No quantitative hepatic adjustment is supplied by this extract.

monitoring: Check hypersensitivity history; obtain drug-specific guidance when organ dysfunction is present.
gaps: No supported renal, hepatic or dialysis schedule here; do not turn missing guidance into a no-adjustment claim. Interaction details not loaded.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Renal table applies to adults and children at least 15 years old; younger children require separate guidance.
contraindications: Known cephalexin or cephalosporin hypersensitivity is contraindicated.

renal.guidance: Label uses CrCl (mL/min): at least 60, no adjustment; 30-59, maximum 1 g/day; 15-29, 250 mg every 8-12 hours; 5-14 without dialysis, 250 mg every 24 hours; 1-4 without dialysis, 250 mg every 48-60 hours.

hepatic.guidance: Renal or hepatic impairment increases prolonged-prothrombin-time risk; monitor patients at risk. No quantitative hepatic schedule is supplied.

interactions: Cephalexin can increase metformin exposure; monitor and consider metformin adjustment.
monitoring: Monitor renal function; reduce dose in renal impairment to limit seizure risk. Monitor prothrombin time in susceptible patients.
gaps: Hemodialysis and renal dosing below age 15 are not established in this label table. Retain CDC immediate-type penicillin-allergy avoidance for the strep lesson.

medication_safety_profiles.population: UCSF adult adjustment guidance; CDC determines the chlamydia regimen and pregnancy exclusions.

renal.guidance: UCSF adult guidance specifies no renal adjustment, including intermittent or continuous hemodialysis.

hepatic.guidance: Rare hepatotoxicity is reported in labeling; no quantitative hepatic schedule is supplied.

interactions: Aluminum/calcium/magnesium antacids and iron reduce absorption. Anticoagulant dosage may need review.
monitoring: Review interacting products and hepatic adverse effects when relevant.
gaps: No validated liver-severity dosing schedule or exact monitoring interval loaded; do not infer unrestricted hepatic safety. Do not generalize adult dosing to children.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Oral tablets; retain the CDC pregnancy-specific chlamydia regimen.
contraindications: Macrolide/ketolide hypersensitivity, or previous azithromycin-associated cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction, is contraindicated.

renal.guidance: No complete renal or dialysis adjustment schedule is included in this profile; do not infer a reduction from pharmacokinetic observations alone.

hepatic.guidance: Hepatic-impairment pharmacokinetics are not established. Severe hepatotoxicity is reported; stop if hepatitis signs or symptoms occur. Prior azithromycin-related liver injury is a contraindication, distinct from general liver impairment.

interactions: Consider QT-prolonging drugs and proarrhythmic conditions. Warfarin requires prothrombin-time monitoring.
monitoring: Review QT risk and symptoms of hepatic injury.
gaps: No Child-Pugh-based dose reduction or dialysis protocol established here.

medication_safety_profiles.population: IM/IV vial safety; CDC, not the older label gonorrhea dose, determines the current STI regimen.
contraindications: Known cephalosporin hypersensitivity is contraindicated. Neonatal contraindications include hyperbilirubinemia and need for IV calcium; do not extend adult teaching to neonates.
Do not give lidocaine-containing ceftriaxone solution intravenously; check lidocaine contraindications before IM use with that diluent.

renal.guidance: Isolated renal impairment generally needs no adjustment at usual adult doses up to 2 g/day. Combined significant renal and hepatic dysfunction requires caution and a maximum of 2 g/day.

hepatic.guidance: Isolated hepatic dysfunction generally needs no adjustment; combined significant renal dysfunction limits dosing to 2 g/day.

interactions: Do not mix or simultaneously infuse with calcium-containing IV solutions. Neonatal restrictions differ.
monitoring: Monitor prothrombin time with low vitamin K stores or impaired synthesis, including chronic hepatic disease.
gaps: The 2 g/day ceiling is not the gonorrhea prescription or a universal maximum for all indications. Do not use older label STI dosing instead of CDC guidance.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Adult IR/ER lessons; formulation-specific starting doses and maxima remain separate.
contraindications: Contraindicated with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, metabolic acidosis including DKA, or hypersensitivity.

renal.guidance: Use eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m2): do not initiate at 30-45; reassess continuation if it falls below 45; discontinue below 30.

hepatic.guidance: Label advises avoiding clinical or laboratory evidence of hepatic disease because of lactic-acidosis risk; this is an avoid-use warning, not a Child-Pugh dose reduction.

interactions: Excess alcohol and drugs increasing metformin accumulation or acidosis risk need review.
monitoring: Check eGFR before starting and at least annually, more often if at risk. Follow the separate contrast-hold instructions when applicable.
gaps: No liver-based reduced-dose regimen is established. This profile is not an exhaustive interaction or contrast protocol.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Adult tablet MDD lesson; do not apply tablet rules to other formulations without checking.
contraindications: MAOIs or use within 14 days of stopping an MAOI, including linezolid/IV methylene blue; pimozide; and sertraline hypersensitivity are contraindications.

renal.guidance: No adjustment for mild through severe renal impairment.

hepatic.guidance: Mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh 5-6): halve the recommended starting dose and therapeutic range/maximum. Moderate or severe hepatic impairment: use is not recommended.

interactions: Other serotonergic drugs increase serotonin-syndrome risk; anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase bleeding risk.
monitoring: Monitor for hyponatremia and serotonin syndrome when relevant; monitor clinical worsening and suicidal thoughts.
gaps: Not recommended in moderate/severe hepatic disease is distinct from a formal section-4 contraindication. No dialysis-specific regimen loaded.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Adult hypertension; renal starting doses depend on indication.
contraindications: Prior ACE-inhibitor angioedema/hypersensitivity or hereditary/idiopathic angioedema; aliskiren with diabetes; neprilysin inhibitors or switching within 36 hours are contraindicated.

renal.guidance: CrCl above 30 mL/min: no adjustment. CrCl 10-30: halve the usual initial dose (hypertension: 5 mg daily). Below 10 or hemodialysis: initial 2.5 mg daily.

hepatic.guidance: Stop for jaundice or marked liver-enzyme elevations and evaluate; no quantitative hepatic dose schedule is provided.

interactions: Potassium-raising drugs and NSAIDs require review.
monitoring: Monitor renal function, potassium and blood pressure. Pregnancy carries a fetal-toxicity warning; discontinue when detected.
gaps: Renal guidance concerns initial dose; titrate only within the supported indication. No hepatic reduced-dose regimen established.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Adult heart-failure lesson; do not substitute cirrhotic-ascites dosing for HF dosing.
contraindications: Hyperkalemia, Addison disease and concomitant eplerenone are contraindicated.

renal.guidance: HF: potassium at most 5 mEq/L and eGFR above 50 mL/min/1.73 m2: initial 25 mg daily. At eGFR 30-50 consider initial 25 mg every other day.

hepatic.guidance: Cirrhosis with ascites: initiate in hospital; fluid/electrolyte shifts can worsen encephalopathy or precipitate coma.

interactions: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium supplements and potassium salt substitutes increase hyperkalemia risk.
monitoring: Check potassium within 1 week of initiation/titration and regularly thereafter; monitor renal function and volume status.
gaps: HF initiation below eGFR 30 or on dialysis needs additional guidance; do not infer safety from omission. Hepatic precautions do not define a Child-Pugh reduction.

medication_safety_profiles.population: Adult AF and VTE lessons; renal rules differ by indication.
contraindications: Active pathological bleeding and severe apixaban hypersensitivity are contraindicated.

renal.guidance: AF: reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily only if at least two: age at least 80, weight at most 60 kg, serum creatinine at least 1.5 mg/dL. Adult VTE labeling recommends no renal adjustment; do not apply AF criteria. ESRD/dialysis and CrCl below 15 lack clinical-trial efficacy/safety data.

hepatic.guidance: Child-Pugh A: no adjustment; B: label cannot provide a dose recommendation; C: not recommended.

interactions: Combined strong P-gp/CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers and other anticoagulants/antiplatelets require the separate labeled interaction pathway.
gaps: No invented Child-Pugh B dose. Dialysis recommendations rely on pharmacokinetics, not demonstrated clinical equivalence. Interaction adjustment rules are not fully loaded.
